<result>## PostHog leadership & engineering quote bank

All quotes verbatim. Handbook pages are company-authored (no byline) — I've marked those. Every URL below returned HTTP 200 on check; HN comments were pulled from the Algolia item API (raw text, not snippets).

---

## 1. "Product engineer" — the core concept

> "Good product engineers: Ship quickly so they have a fast feedback loop • Understand the company strategy, and prioritize based on this _and_ what they believe users want • Can easily propose ideas for what to build • Make sure the things they've built are being used • Follow up after they've built something to improve it if needed • Are good at descoping things and getting products or features into people's hands quickly • Have users that they're friendly with • Manage to build things without lots of internal meetings • Dive _deep_ when they need to, because shipping D might also require solving A, B, and C"
— PostHog handbook, "How to do product, as an engineer", https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/product-engineering

> "Bad product engineers: Consider research something that takes two weeks rather than two hours • Can't explain our company strategy • Can't explain who their product is built for • Don't know their product's competitors • Only work on things they've been told to work on • Don't know the names of any of their users • Never challenge why they're being told to work on something • Don't talk to users about what they're going to build, or what they've built • Don't track if the things they've built are being used • Spend 6 months on a huge feature before a user can try it • Never remove features or complexity… • Focus on internal alignment over company strategy and what users need • Wait for someone else to fix an adjacent problem"
— same page. **This is the single most dashboard-relevant artifact PostHog has published — it is effectively their impact rubric.**

> "A product engineer decides what to build. As opposed to someone who follows a product requirements doc."
— James Hawkins, *Untrapping Product Teams* podcast writeup, https://dpereira.substack.com/p/no-babysitters-no-bottlenecks-inside — 10 Jul 2025

> "Instead of providing a product manager who tells the engineers what to build, we're trying to help our engineers be good product managers."
— James Hawkins, *Truth, Lies & Work* EP 189, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 Apr 2025

> "The concept internally is a 'product engineer' – i.e. an engineer who is product-minded and autonomous, rather than mindlessly filing tickets."
— James Hawkins, "How we designed our company for speed", https://posthog.com/founders/how-come-we-ship-so-much — 1 Nov 2023

> "Product engineers – sometimes referred to as product-minded engineers – 'own' **the product** and are responsible for its successes and failures… In contrast, software engineers 'own' **the code they write**."
— Ian Vanagas & Jina Yoon, https://posthog.com/blog/product-engineer-vs-software-engineer — 8 Dec 2025

> "Drivers not passengers. Proactive people that can fully own projects and get them done (or make sure they get help) are what we need… people who can take high-level requirements, decide what to build, do so with customers, and keep iterating."
— PostHog handbook, "Strong team", https://posthog.com/handbook/strong-team

---

## 2. Measuring / evaluating engineers — and what they explicitly reject

**The Weave section of the management handbook is the most directly on-point thing PostHog has ever published about engineering metrics:**

> "We use a tool called Weave to collect stats for engineers. Engineers can log in to see their numbers and those of other engineers."
> "We understand that all the work an engineer does can't be properly represented in a tool that just looks at PR output. Data in Weave is _not_ the decision-maker for whether someone is succeeding in their role at PostHog. It can be, however, a part of the conversation."
> "We use Weave to: Look for outliers in the company in terms of output (both high and low - sometimes unexpected people are rising to the top!) • Watch for issues with overall team productivity to identify possible blockers • Start conversations with team leads"
> "We don't use Weave to: Make a decision to let someone go… • Monitor your PRs - our management layer is stretched way too thin to micromanage this • Creep on your use of AI - we don't care how or if you use AI to get a job done, as long as it gets done • Make a call on how valuable someone is - some people with low PR output are very valuable to the company, and we're 100% aware that things like heavy support load can impact output"
> "We have compared statistics in Weave against other (imperfect!) metrics that can be used to gauge productivity, such as number of commits, number of PRs, total github activity, etc, and see similar patterns amongst them… In addition, it gives engineers access to the same information we have about them, so using it increases transparency."
— PostHog handbook, "Managers and management", https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management

> "if X was leaving for a similar role at another company, would you try to keep them?" … "Dig in where the answer is 'no' - what would it take for this to be a 'yes'?"
> Team leads are asked: "i. Is the person a driver or a passenger? ii. Does this person get things done proactively? iii. Are they optimistic by default?"
— PostHog handbook, same page (the keeper test)

> "Keeper tests are not designed to replace direct feedback… If you have feedback for someone, give it to them directly – don't rely on the keeper test to do it for you."
— PostHog handbook, "Feedback", https://posthog.com/handbook/people/feedback

> "A checklist of things / a formal career progression framework — This is self-interested by its nature, so creates the wrong incentives. The benefits of frameworks only start to outweigh their drawbacks when you need to start coordinating 100s of people."
— PostHog handbook, "Career progression", https://posthog.com/handbook/people/career-progression

> "Level does not correlate with increased importance, but with impact within PostHog. Your level is _not_ a title… Senior: owns and drives high-impact projects or a whole product, decides what needs to happen and does everything necessary to get that done. Staff: same as senior, but also _consistently_ owns and drives large projects that impact the entire company, not just their product, team or even function."
— PostHog handbook, "Compensation", https://posthog.com/handbook/people/compensation

> "In 2022, we required 'OKRs' as part of quarterly planning, but eventually walked it back. We found engineers were agonizing over finding the right metrics, while also feeling like metrics didn't accurately reflect their subjective view of progress."
> "We learned that setting OKRs just because 'Google does it' doesn't mean it's the right thing to do."
— Ian Vanagas, "You're doing quarterly planning wrong", https://posthog.com/newsletter/quarterly-planning-mistakes — 30 Jun 2025

> "All objectives are bad - they have many compromises, are fallible, easy to game, or may be affected by external factors, so use the least bad ones."
> "Use metrics only if they help you. Goals should be primarily output-based - the actual things that we will do and build."
— PostHog handbook, "Setting quarterly goals", https://posthog.com/handbook/company/goal-setting

> "We used to do OKRs and metric-based goals, but we ran into two problems with it: 1. Teams wasted too much time coming up with the right metric to focus on. 2. Engineers focused on small quick wins to move those metrics, rather than building what our users actually wanted."
— James Hawkins & Lior Neu-ner, "Product management is broken. Engineers can fix it", https://posthog.com/newsletter/product-management-is-broken — 3 Dec 2024

> "We prefer goals orientated around what teams will ship, rather than more abstract goals like 'increase conversions by 10%'."
— James Temperton, "The magic of small engineering teams", https://posthog.com/newsletter/small-teams — 3 Jul 2024

> "How do you know the team are doing this? What process do we implement? None! The moment you implement a process to do so, you're re-creating the doom loop you're trying to avoid. Resist your urge to 'trust, but verify'."
— James Hawkins, "The deadline doom loop", https://posthog.com/newsletter/deadline-doom-loop — 9 Jan 2025

> "Setting deadlines, creating arbitrary reporting obligations, or saying 'if you ship X, you will get to Y title' are examples of trying to use extrinsic motivation. This is un-cracked."
— Charles Cook, "Hiring (and managing) cracked engineers", https://posthog.com/founders/cracked-manifesto — 23 May 2024

> "The 20% of your team who are underperforming will take up 80% of your effort. • You may be able to get an underperformer's output from 4/10 to 6/10 if you work hard with them. • Doubling down on a cracked person's performance can improve their output from 8/10 to 9/10. • It's the 9/10 quality output that will delight your users, so you should focus on that, even if the absolute increase in performance is less."
— Charles Cook, same piece

> "one of the most interesting learnings so far from the data we've seen (~400 developers using it for the last month to log issues in their code/processes, >1,000 survey responses) is that the average developer encountering an issue loses more than twice as much time in Planning and Deployment than in Writing Code."
— James Hawkins (HN: `james_impliu`), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21750586 — 10 Dec 2019

**What they DO measure per product** (small-team growth reviews): MRR/ARR, MoM growth rate, revenue expansion/contraction/churn, quarterly NRR, unique monthly users + growth rate, activation, 1/3/6-month usage retention, 4-week NPS, created tickets, escalated tickets + SLA, ratio of users vs. tickets. — PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/product/metrics

> "The product small team is responsible for everything related to their area, particularly: 1. Usage 2. Quality 3. Revenue"
— PostHog handbook, "Small teams", https://posthog.com/handbook/company/small-teams

---

## 3. Shipping fast, ship early, speed vs. quality

> "Merge anytime. Friday afternoon? Merge. Our testing, reviewing and building process should be good enough that we're comfortable merging any time."
— PostHog handbook, "Shipping & releasing", https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/development-process

> "One rule we try to stick to is one pull request per developer per day. That can sometimes mean a Work In Progress, but it always means something goes into the repo."
> "Many new features are so simple they can verge on embarrassing. That's how they should feel when they're launched to the first users, if you have a forgiving initial audience."
> "It's better to spend a week building something and learning no one cares rather than losing a month polishing the wheels on the moon-buggy when it turns out that Earth is pretty cool anyway."
— "We ship whenever", https://posthog.com/blog/we-ship-whenever — 23 Jul 2020

> "If given a choice, go live. If you can't go live, reduce the task size so you can. • We are small, and can only win based on speed and agility. • Going live forces a level of completion, on which you can build."
— PostHog handbook, "Culture", https://posthog.com/handbook/company/culture

> "Shipping fast should feel a little dangerous, chaotic, and scary sometimes. It's an anti-pattern to want complete consensus, or control."
> "We accept this because shipping fast gets us information from our users, and the market, more quickly than shipping perfect. TL;DR: The faster we learn, the faster our product improves. Speed, like talent, compounds."
— Andy Vandervell, "This is why you're not shipping", https://posthog.com/newsletter/this-is-why-youre-not-shipping — 3 Apr 2025

> "And we concluded, like, we're not going to win on design polish here. We're going to win on engineering velocity. So the entire company is designed to ship quickly."
> "our preferred method of communication from an engineer is not to spend ages like super validating your product, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. Just build something real, ship it."
— James Hawkins, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 Apr 2025

> "I feel like a weird industry has popped up that makes you feel like you can validate everything in advance. I think this comes from Product Managers in large, risk-averse companies that excessively try to minimize mistakes. However, if you want to start a startup, you aren't optimizing for mistake minimization! You are figuring out if anyone cares as quickly as possible."
— James Hawkins (HN: `james_impliu`), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36584166 — 4 Jul 2023

> "Despite what the industry tells you, it's debatable how well you can validate ideas up front… Just shipping is often the best way to validate an idea."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/product-engineering

> "We'd prefer you ship ten things quickly (and make a couple of mistakes) than plan too much. You will tend to gather more information by _doing_ rather than _planning_."
— PostHog handbook, "Building a world-class engineering environment", https://posthog.com/handbook/world-class-engineering

> "Frequently, you'll hear our engineers asking each other 'what's stopping us from putting this into a user's hands now?'"
— James Hawkins, https://posthog.com/newsletter/deadline-doom-loop — 9 Jan 2025

> "We've always cared more about making it easy to quickly fix things rather than avoiding breaking them in the first place… It's much more important that we find out if the change is actually useful instead of wasting time getting it perfect on the first try."
— Paul D'Ambra, "10,000 PRs a month is easy", https://posthog.com/blog/10k-prs-a-month — 28 Jul 2026

> "If users can't adopt what you ship, it's not velocity, it's waste."
> "You're no longer constrained by your capacity to ship new things, but by your users' capacity to adopt them."
— Cleo Lant, "The hidden danger of shipping fast", https://posthog.com/newsletter/hidden-danger-of-shipping-fast — 9 Feb 2026 *(the one internal counterweight to pure throughput)*

---

## 4. Autonomy, no managers, don't ask permission, ownership

> "We hire people that are really great at their jobs, and get out of their way. There are no deadlines, very minimal coordination and you won't have us breathing down your neck. In return, we ask for extraordinarily high ownership."
> "_Why not now?_ means getting things done _proactively_, _today_. You do not need consensus to do things… You certainly shouldn't wait until next quarter if your new idea makes more sense to work on than your previous goal."
> "Default to _not_ asking for permission to do something if you are acting in the best interests of PostHog."
— PostHog handbook, "Values", https://posthog.com/handbook/values (last line from https://posthog.com/handbook/company/culture)

> "Engineers decide what to build… If an engineer at PostHog believes they should work on X, they can build X."
> "One of the things we've learned is the very strongest engineers are usually those who want autonomy the most, and so freedom is a great way to attract and retain world-class talent."
> "80% of the company are shipping product."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/world-class-engineering

> "A manager at PostHog is _not_ responsible for: … 2. Setting tasks for your direct reports… 5. 'Approving,' whether that's projects, expenses, days off, or accounts - people should have admin access by default to most things"
> "Management is intentionally spread thin at PostHog. This is a forcing function for making sure that teams and ICs continue to have high levels of autonomy. Bored managers are micromanagers."
> "What managers should aim for at PostHog is to make themselves obsolete."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management

> "The most important thing we've built at PostHog came from an engineer deciding what to build… Karl disagreed and built it anyway. It ended up being wildly popular with customers, and changed our entire company strategy! … And all this because a single engineer disagreed with the CEO."
> "At PostHog, PMs no longer own the roadmap, make product decisions, or shield engineers from users or the wider business goals. Instead, our engineers run the show."
> "We think of PMs as the team's compass. They don't decide the destination…"
> "A giant checklist of processes and reviews is a tell-tale sign that a company doesn't trust their engineers. This is an anti-pattern."
— James Hawkins & Lior Neu-ner, https://posthog.com/newsletter/product-management-is-broken — 3 Dec 2024

> "I'm 100% certain our company would not be as successful had I been able to control everything anyway… our most impactful ever idea was going from one product to 2 products. And that came from an individual developer having the freedom to just build what he wanted."
> "The biggest challenge is, it's not everyone fighting to be the manager, it's people fighting to not be the manager."
> "we'd rather have some risk-taking over what gets built in an extremely low consensus environment is our preferred way of building stuff."
— James Hawkins, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 Apr 2025

> "we are growing through more autonomy and transparency not through process."
— Tim Glaser (HN: `timgl`), recurring line in PostHog's *Ask HN: Who is hiring?* posts, e.g. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47980397 — 1 May 2026

> "If you find yourself approving stuff for your team because of your position as their manager, remove yourself from the process."
> "Long approval processes that exist for the sake of having someone senior sign off on something in order to kick accountability up the chain? Very un-cracked."
— Charles Cook, https://posthog.com/founders/cracked-manifesto — 23 May 2024

> "'You're the driver' is a key value for us at PostHog. We aim to hire people who are great at their jobs and get out of their way. No deadlines, minimal coordination, and no managers telling you what to do."
> "Every time you see ✨ collaboration ✨ happening, speak up and destroy it. Say 'there are too many people involved. X, you are the driver, you decide.'"
> "Default to shipping. Pull requests > issues > Slack messages."
— Charles Cook, "Collaboration sucks", https://posthog.com/newsletter/collaboration-sucks — 11 Nov 2025

> "You'll know you're successful if: You can disappear for two weeks without affecting the quality and frequency of releases."
> "Aim for 80–90% of your week in the codebase."
— Lior Neu-ner, "Engineering lead failure modes", https://posthog.com/newsletter/tech-lead-failure-modes — 4 Aug 2025

> "The magic of small teams isn't just about speed – it's about ownership. When six or fewer people own a problem, there's nowhere to hide and no way to pass the buck."
— James Hawkins & Lior Neu-ner, https://posthog.com/newsletter/product-management-is-broken

> "product engineers should never be in more than one team because this acts against proper ownership."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/small-teams

---

## 5. Hiring / "10x" / cracked engineers

> "10x engineers are idealized for their incredible technical skills that fuel progress, but if they are working on the wrong things, a product isn't 10x more likely to succeed."
> Six traits they look for: "1. Always prototyping and experimenting … 2. Comfortable writing … 3. A genuine love for building … 4. Customer obsessed … 5. Understands the broader context … 6. Easy to work with"
> "We look for drivers, not passengers. People who can go from idea to finished feature without managers telling them what to do."
> "the best sort of communication at PostHog is a pull request. Other companies encourage piling tasks on other people's plates. We try to figure it out ourselves and open a PR if possible (even if it is wrong)."
> "Because we believe talent compounds, it is worth the extra work to find someone with top-tier technical skills as well as the traits listed here."
— Ian Vanagas, "Beyond the 10x engineer", https://posthog.com/newsletter/beyond-the-10x-engineer — 8 Feb 2024

> "Cracked engineers apply themselves to the craft of building products with a quasi-religious fervor, and love what they do." … "Joy comes from the craft itself, not creating shareholder value."
> "There is no number of years of experience that correlates with crackedness, in either direction."
> "You don't need to have worked at a FAANG/MAMAA/shit-hot SV-based company. We welcome cracked engineers who held together failing companies – we like their paranoia."
> "The **number one** thing you can do to motivate cracked people? Find them more cracked people to work with! … Conversely, the number one thing you can do to demotivate them is to make them work with un-cracked people."
> "Do the stuff that arrogant senior people would find 'boring'. Write tests. Respond to customer support queries. Go weirdly deep into some piece of analysis."
— Charles Cook, https://posthog.com/founders/cracked-manifesto — 23 May 2024

> "the thing we're prioritizing for an engineer in the SuperDay is how much useful stuff can you build basically in a day?" … "There's remarkable difference between what candidates say and what they do."
> "the kind of person that would be very happy working at Google is probably going to be really unhappy working at PostHog because they won't have any, they'll just like, there's no boundaries or spoonfeeding or resources available to them"
> "One of the ways to not get hired at PostHog is to say, I want to manage loads of people."
— James Hawkins, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 Apr 2025

> "As I tell people during interviews, being an engineer at PostHog is like driving a car. If you like driving – i.e. being actively engaged and adjusting to feedback from the road (users) – it's fun. But you can't nap. You must stay switched on as no one will spoon-feed you product requirements."
— James Hawkins, https://posthog.com/newsletter/deadline-doom-loop — 9 Jan 2025

> "For everyone on the PostHog team meeting a candidate, ask yourself – will this person raise the bar at PostHog? The answer should be yes if we want to hire them."
> "if it is not a _definite yes_, then it's a _no_."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/people/hiring-process

> "In the words of James Greenhill: 'If it's not a hell yes, it's a hell no.'"
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/small-teams

> "We know that exceptional people are usually spiky, they don't have an evenly distributed skill set so people can have reservations about a certain area and they can still be exceptional."
— PostHog handbook, "Talent", https://posthog.com/handbook/people/talent

> "The task is designed to be _too much_ work for one person to complete in a day, in order to get a sense of their ability to prioritize (and ship!)."
> "Has built something from scratch, ideally with minimal outside help… User-centric: Our engineering team work very closely with our users – they do customer support, demos, and help with implementation."
— PostHog handbook, "Engineering Hiring", https://posthog.com/handbook/people/hiring-process/engineering-hiring

> "Focus on slope … and be very wary of getting seduced by companies rather than people. Candidates who've worked at places with strong product market fit will have had an easier time achieving results. Some of our best people have come from a string of very average startups."
> "Did they drive the project or were they a passenger? Who actually wrote the code?"
— PostHog handbook, "Interview technique", https://posthog.com/handbook/people/hiring-process/how-to-interview

> "26. 90% of culture is getting hiring right in the first place. You cannot make an uncracked engineer cracked."
> "31. Hire fewer people in general. Excess hiring is often a sign that you haven't worked out some part of your culture."
> "33. Most of your hiring metrics are vanity metrics. Don't hide behind a conversion funnel, do good work consistently on the inputs."
> "12. Take home tasks are pointless in an AI world."
— Charles Cook, "43 things we've learned about hiring at PostHog", https://posthog.com/newsletter/43-lessons-about-hiring-for-startups — 11 Apr 2025

> "Actual work is 10x more valuable than interviews"
> "many of the best people at PostHog worked at or founded companies that just didn't work. We find this cultivates a degree of grit and optimism that's invaluable in a startup"
— Andy Vandervell, https://posthog.com/newsletter/hiring-at-posthog-lessons — 7 Sep 2023

> "The best applicants are ones who are existing users and who really are interested in the product, versus those who are doing a pull request to stand out."
— James Hawkins (HN: `james_impliu`), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32863754 — 16 Sep 2022

> "You mean Product Engineers? We've hired ~80 people in that role in the last year!"
— Tim Glaser (HN: `timgl`), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48225663 — 21 May 2026

> "We proactively reward those that do these things, not those that self-promote."
> "Getting our brand on your resumé. If you join for self-promotion, you (ironically) won't do well!"
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/strong-team

---

## 6. Dogfooding, talking to customers, working in the open

> "We have a simple theory about building successful products: the people building them should be as close to people using them as possible… Engineers in this scenario get a sanitized version of the truth."
> "Think of user interviews like automated tests… a short-term investment in your long-term productivity."
— Ian Vanagas, "An engineer's guide to talking to users", https://posthog.com/newsletter/talk-to-users — 25 Apr 2024

> "Product engineers do support at PostHog. They log into Zendesk, respond to users, debug their issues, and ship fixes."
> "When building, it encourages engineers to write reliable and maintainable code, because they will be the ones who need to fix it if it breaks."
— Ian Vanagas, "Doing support makes you a better engineer", https://posthog.com/newsletter/engineers-do-support — 29 Aug 2024

> "any kind of feedback, bug report, complaint or usage is a gift from users."
> "Closing the loop is the final point. If a user gives feedback or asks for something, you should ultimately respond with: A PR (which will likely delight them) / A roadmap item… / A reason why we can't do their thing"
> "Look for evidence that users have _actually done anything_ about the problems they say they have."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/product-engineering

> "in the early days, it was about trust… I thought, well, transparency is kind of the foundation of trust."
> "if you know that you'll get like angry mobs on the internet talking about your like policies around hiring or firing people or whatever it might be, it just means you have to be a bit more rigorous in how you think through stuff."
— James Hawkins, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 Apr 2025

> "Knowing that thousands of people will read our handbook pages forces clearer thinking."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/values

> "Dogfooding: Use the product yourself. When you see something that annoys you, fix it."
— PostHog handbook, https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/development-process

> "Every team member should be dogfooding the product - not just the product manager. This improves your collective autonomy when it comes to prioritizing which features to build."
— Marcus Hyett, "The importance of dogfooding", https://posthog.com/blog/dogfooding — 13 Sep 2021

> "Everything we do is out in the open. Team goals. Product revenue. Growth reviews. Sprint issues. The decisions people make and why. It's all out there. This makes us faster because it forces individuals to decide for themselves if they need to stay informed."
— Andy Vandervell, https://posthog.com/newsletter/this-is-why-youre-not-shipping — 3 Apr 2025

> "Every quarter we all get to read the same income statements investors do."
— Danilo Campos, "PostHog ruined all other jobs for me", https://posthog.com/blog/uh-i-like-my-job — 14 Jan 2025

---

## 7. AI coding agents changing engineering

> "In the last 6 months, we've gone from shipping 1,441 PRs in January to 4,725 PRs in June while increasing engineering headcount by only 10%."
> "More PRs isn't a good thing in and of itself. It happens as a result of hiring talented, driven people and investing in agentic automation."
> "There's no token budget set by some higher-ups at PostHog… It's up to them as individuals to use the right amount of tokens, and none of us are going to pretend we know what that amount is."
> "Over the last 4 months, we moved from around 20% of our monorepo PRs being opened by agent to 70%."
> "Line count is a rough proxy for quality. Less is better as past some threshold people stop reviewing carefully and quality drops."
> "the percentage of reverts has barely changed, and we are eager to revert whenever we need to. This is a sign production isn't breaking more under the load of agentic PRs."
> "20% of our PRs are approved by StampHog and it only costs us about $300 per month in tokens."
> "Simple reviews have become like linting. Humans shouldn't be doing either."
> Human reviewers should focus on: "Do I understand this change? / Does the author understand the change? / Is this change safe? / Is this change valuable?"
— Paul D'Ambra, "10,000 PRs a month is easy: How devex is evolving at PostHog", https://posthog.com/blog/10k-prs-a-month — 28 Jul 2026 **(the closest thing PostHog has to a public engineering-metrics dashboard)**

> "Human reviewers should focus on things agents are bad at: Does this solve the right problem for customers? Is this the right thing to build at all?… The author still owns correctness: reviewers help reduce risk, but approval does not move responsibility away from the person responsible for the PR."
— PostHog handbook, "How we review PRs", https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/how-we-review

> "Agents are writing code faster than any human can review. The naive solution would be for developers to review code faster. The 500 IQ take is for developers to review as little code as possible."
— Jina Yoon, "Stop being the code review bottleneck", https://posthog.com/newsletter/code-review-tips — 9 Jul 2026

> "PostHog is just a little further than that with agents writing about 70% of our PRs, but humans still skim at least 80% of those."
— Jina Yoon, "Can software factories actually work?", https://posthog.com/newsletter/software-factories — 11 Aug 2026

> "Everyone agreed on one thing though: coding with AI is a skill. It takes practice and a lot of mistakes to get good at it."
— Ian Vanagas, "Avoid these AI coding mistakes", https://posthog.com/newsletter/ai-coding-mistakes — 30 Sep 2025

> "when it comes to hiring, AI-native beats experience. Not 'experienced person who uses AI.'… Years of experience are now the tiebreaker between two AI-native candidates, not the gate that decides who gets to the table."
> "PostHog's hiring plan for the next 2-3 years is smaller than it would have been a year ago. Not because we're growing slower. Because each AI-native hire is cracked enough that we need fewer of them."
> Screening questions: "Walk me through a workflow you built or replicated… What's the best AI workflow you've stolen from somebody else?… What's the biggest failed experiment you've had with AI?"
— Fraser Hopper, "Being AI-native matters more than experience", https://posthog.com/blog/ai-native-hiring — 19 May 2026

> "Last week, the majority of dashboards were created by agents via PostHog AI, MCP, our API, or our onboarding wizard."
> "We want to solve the low-level tasks in building software, the less creative but important work, so you can spend more time on high impact work."
— James Hawkins, "PostHog's next chapter", https://posthog.com/blog/posthogs-next-chapter — 1 May 2026

> "I rewrote PostHog's SQL parser using multiple long-running Claude Code sessions in parallel. The result was 16K lines of 'hand'-rolled parser code, 5K lines of tooling, a few more K of tests, and a ~70x speed up."
> "It took about 2 days to get a proof of concept, and about a week to get something I could ship to production." (HN: `robbie-c`, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48664983)
— Robbie Coomber, https://posthog.com/blog/sql-parser — 24 Jun 2026

> "Two marketers have shipped real changes to a genuinely complex codebase." *(paraphrase-free version:)* "That's how Joe and I – two marketers – have shipped real changes to a genuinely complex codebase."
— Cleo Lant, "Everything (and everyone) is build mode now", https://posthog.com/blog/everything-is-build-mode — 15 Jun 2026

---

## Bonus: structural facts worth putting on a dashboard

- **Small teams:** "A small team should _strictly_ be between 2-6 people." / "A small team has the final call in which of its features get into production, with no need for external QA/control." / "A small team must have a customer (internal or external)." — https://posthog.com/handbook/company/small-teams
- **Team-lead accountability metric:** monthly per-product growth reviews asking "Are our 10 biggest customers happy users of the product?… Why was churn high last month?" — https://posthog.com/newsletter/product-management-is-broken
- **PR sizing norm:** "PRs should ideally be sized to be doable in one day, including code review and QA." — https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/development-process
- **Deep work:** "meeting-free days every Tuesday and Thursday" — https://posthog.com/handbook/world-class-engineering
- **Severance / decisiveness:** "We offer four months severance when we let people go for performance reasons" — https://posthog.com/handbook/strong-team
- **No PIPs:** "We avoid performance improvement plans because it's demeaning for those affected, and excessively time-consuming for managers." — https://posthog.com/newsletter/this-is-why-youre-not-shipping

## Design implication for the dashboard (the tension to design around)

PostHog's own writing sets up a trap for any engineering-impact dashboard: they run one (Weave, plus GitHub data streamed into PostHog), but every published statement hedges it — output stats are "a part of the conversation," never the decision-maker; low PR count can mean high support load; "more PRs isn't a good thing in and of itself." Meanwhile their *actual* impact rubric is the good/bad product engineer list (shipped things being used, follow-up, users you know by name, descoping) and per-product Usage/Quality/Revenue. A dashboard that leads with PR/commit throughput will read as un-cracked to this audience; one that pairs throughput with *shipped-thing adoption*, revert rate, support-load context, and per-product usage/revenue/NPS matches what they already say they believe.

**Two notes on sourcing:** James Hawkins's HN username is `james_impliu` (not `jamesefhawkins`, which doesn't exist); Tim Glaser is `timgl`. I found no verifiable verbatim @james406 X threads — nitter mirrors are dead and the quotes I could see were unattributable, so I omitted them rather than risk a bad citation.</result>

---
date: "2026-07-28"
title: "10,000 PRs a month is easy: How devex is evolving at PostHog"
author:
  - paul-dambra
rootPage: /blog
sidebar: Blog
featuredImage: >-
  https://res.cloudinary.com/dmukukwp6/image/upload/stop_being_the_code_review_bottleneck_hero_a734a37558.png
featuredImageType: full
showTitle: true
hideAnchor: true
category: Engineering
tags:
  - AI
  - Engineering
---

Shipping cadence is accelerating at PostHog. In the last 6 months, we've gone from shipping 1,441 PRs in January to 4,725 PRs in June while increasing engineering headcount by only 10%.

![More PRs](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmukukwp6/image/upload/w_1600,c_limit,q_auto,f_auto/Clean_Shot_2026_07_23_at_15_27_38_2x_1a2d8df53b.png)

This is heading towards our north star for internal developer experience: "10,000 PRs a month is easy." We thought we would have until December to hit this number, but we might get there as early as September.

More PRs isn't a good thing in and of itself. It happens as a result of hiring talented, driven people and investing in agentic automation. Even if we don't hit these numbers, working toward our goals means making local dev, CI, and validation faster and better.

Here's how we've increased the volume of engineering work while still delivering reliable systems, and the changes we're making to make sure this remains the case.

## Where has this acceleration come from?

The simple answer: people using AI a lot more.

There's no token budget set by some higher-ups at PostHog. We want people to figure out how we _make use of new tools_ and _create new tools_. It's up to them as individuals to use the right amount of tokens, and none of us are going to pretend we know what that amount is. 

This works because it's a big part of our culture to value trust and feedback over process. If we get to the point where we're uncomfortable with someone's spend, we'll dig into that with them and figure out if the spend is reasonable. Everyone else can learn from that too.

Everybody's using agents and [writing skills](/newsletter/writing-agent-skills), but our [self-driving loop](/newsletter/loops) is further fueling the accelerated cadence. Over the last 4 months, we moved from around 20% of our monorepo PRs being opened by agent to 70%. [Self-driving](/blog/self-driving-product) is around 4% of our PRs right now but growing fast.

Speeding up the rate we create PRs doesn't necessarily mean speeding up the rate we can handle them. For that, we're relying on agentic loops getting those PRs ready for human attention. Things like: 

- Keeping up to date with [trunk](/product-engineers/trunk-based-development)
- Making sure that CI is passing
- Making sure that reviews have been acted on

The folks who are pushing the limits of what they can achieve have written their own applications, like [review](/newsletter/code-review-tips) and PR management tools or [`qa-swarm`](https://github.com/pauldambra/dotfiles/tree/main/ai/skills/qa-swarm) and [`babysit-prs`](https://github.com/haacked/dotfiles/blob/main/ai/skills/babysit-prs/SKILL.md) skills. They have maybe 40 PRs open at the same time, but we want to push this further and get more people on board. Something like 60% of my token spend is burned automating the toil of handling CI and review and I don't regret a single dollar.

## Getting off local machines

The PostHog stack is very heavy for local development, so we've always needed powerful dev machines. This was fine until people started wanting to run multiple copies of the stack to test PRs. We're hitting the limits of what's possible now; there's only so much RAM and disk you can put into a MacBook.

So, we're building out cloud dev machines. They're skill-driven so you just ask your agent to start a dev machine with a prompt like: 

> Start a dev box, run this PR in it, and record me a video of the changes that we're making so I can see the output of the test.

This is powered by our internal developer CLI [`hogli`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/tree/master/tools/hogli), which also pushes CI checks down into local dev by helping agents better test code locally. === career-progression, full ===
**Give you loads of autonomy**

We don't limit you, and will push for much more than you may think is possible. It will feel hard, but rewarding. You will get used to not asking for approval.

**Give you lots of interesting problems to work on**

PostHog has a wide variety of challenges - from data, to entire new products and features, to design and UX tradeoffs. On the go-to-market side, we're wildly different - you'll learn about self serve, bottom up adoption, handling a community, and how giving things away for free leads to us making money.

We have [small teams](/handbook/team-structure) - we can move people around as we grow to provide variety and to let people switch up their focus if things get stale.

**Lightweight management**

You have [someone to talk to](/handbook/company/management), but without being micromanaged. Their priority is to support you, and we give them resources to make them a better manager. They will also do a [regular career check-in](/handbook/company/management#1-1s-and-team-member-growth) with you as part of your 1-1s to ensure you're on the right track. 

**Build a huge open source portfolio**

Better than a fancy title - you can show future employers or investors what you built and the problems you solved.

**Your team around you see your everyday work more than a manager - get direct feedback from them**

Great people + [direct feedback](/handbook/people/feedback) = learning.

## Ways we do not help you progress

**A checklist of things / a formal career progression framework**

This is self-interested by its nature, so creates the wrong incentives. The benefits of frameworks only start to outweigh their drawbacks when you need to start coordinating 100s of people. 

**Fancy titles**

We don't have a wide range of titles - we want people to be as equal as possible in order to enable autonomy versus micromanagement. Your open source work speaks for itself.

**Getting a manager to progress you**

This gives too much power to managers. No one else can really do this for you - your motivation to progress has to be intrinsic to be sustainable.

118-Quarterly planning is only as useful as the progress you make on it. If you're not checking in on your progress, you can't know if you'll be successful.

Verified. Here is the addendum — new material only, plus two corrections to what I delivered earlier.

---

# Addendum: material additions and corrections

## The best new source: PostHog published their own engineering metrics

**"10,000 PRs a month is easy: How devex is evolving at PostHog"** — Paul D'Ambra, 28 Jul 2026, https://posthog.com/blog/10k-prs-a-month

I verified this in full. It is the single most citable artifact for your dashboard, because it is PostHog publicly reporting engineering throughput *and* publicly hedging it in the same breath.

> "In the last 6 months, we've gone from shipping 1,441 PRs in January to 4,725 PRs in June while increasing engineering headcount by only 10%."
> "This is heading towards our north star for internal developer experience: **'10,000 PRs a month is easy.'**"
> "**More PRs isn't a good thing in and of itself.** It happens as a result of hiring talented, driven people and investing in agentic automation."
> "Over the last 4 months, **we moved from around 20% of our monorepo PRs being opened by agent to 70%.** Self-driving is around 4% of our PRs right now but growing fast."
> "There's no token budget set by some higher-ups at PostHog... It's up to them as individuals to use the right amount of tokens, and none of us are going to pretend we know what that amount is."

**Their published quality proxies — copy these, they are pre-approved:**

> "The first is size. **Line count is a rough proxy for quality. Less is better** as past some threshold people stop reviewing carefully and quality drops."

| Percentile | Wk of May 25 | Wk of Jul 13 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| p50 | 120 | 144 | +20% |
| p75 | 398 | 760 | +91% |
| p90 | 1,004 | 1,432 | +43% |
| p99 | 7,718 | 14,023 | +82% |

> "Another way to judge quality is through PR titles. We use conventional commits like `fix`, `feat`, and `revert`... The distribution of PR types is stable across the last year. AI isn't just creating more fixes or refactors. More importantly, **the percentage of reverts has barely changed, and we are eager to revert whenever we need to. This is a sign production isn't breaking more under the load of agentic PRs.**"

Merged PRs/month went 755 (May 2025) → 1,126 (Nov 2025) → 4,868 (Jun 2026), with `fix` holding ~41%, `feat` ~36%, `revert` ~0.2% throughout.

> "20% of our PRs are approved by StampHog and it only costs us about $300 per month in tokens."
> "We've always cared more about making it easy to quickly fix things rather than avoiding breaking them in the first place."
> "in June 2026, we used 21,643,653 minutes of CI time. That's 41 *years* of CI time in a single month."

**Their four human-review questions** (from the same post, and the best candidate for a "review quality" dimension): *Do I understand this change? Does the author understand the change? Is this change safe? Is this change valuable?* Plus: "Simple reviews have become like linting. Humans shouldn't be doing either."

Companion piece, Jina Yoon: "Agents are writing code faster than any human can review. The naive solution would be for developers to review code faster. **The 500 IQ take is for developers to review as little code as possible.**" — https://posthog.com/newsletter/code-review-tips

---

## Measured data on the repo, as of today

Sampled live from the GitHub API on 2026-09-02:

- **5,199 merged PRs in the last 30 days** (~200–310 per weekday, ~20–30 per weekend day). **26,626 merged YTD 2026.**
- In an unbiased 500-PR sample (2026-08-31 → 09-02): **86% carry the `## 🤖 Agent context` section**; **65% "Human-driven (agent-assisted)"**, **20% "Fully autonomous"**; only ~14% claim to be fully human-authored.
- **`Co-authored-by` trailer: 3%. "Generated with Claude Code" boilerplate: 1%** — because the PR template explicitly forbids decorative human co-authorship.
- **93% list which `/skills` were invoked.**
- Bot accounts are 13% of merges (`posthog[bot]` etc.) and ship real product work, not chores.

**The finding that should drive your data model:** of the 98 "Fully autonomous" PRs in that sample, **49 came from bot accounts and 49 came from human GitHub accounts** — agents running under an engineer's token. So GitHub author tells you almost nothing. **The `**Autonomy:**` line in the PR body is the only reliable authorship signal in this repo**, and the PR assignee is the only reliable human-accountability signal.

That is a stronger version of what I said earlier: not merely "prefer assignee over author" but "author is actively misleading here, ~10% of the time in the autonomous direction alone."

---

## New material for §5 (measuring engineers)

Three findings that sharpen the warning considerably.

**1. PostHog tried metric-based goals and abandoned them, citing gaming.** — https://posthog.com/newsletter/quarterly-planning-mistakes (section header is literally "Obsessing over metrics")
> "In 2022, we required 'OKRs' as part of quarterly planning, but eventually walked it back. We found engineers were agonizing over finding the right metrics, while also feeling like metrics didn't accurately reflect their subjective view of progress."
> "We learned that setting OKRs just because 'Google does it' doesn't mean it's the right thing to do."
> "Some might say these goals are 'too vague' or 'don't count as OKRs.' Our response is that they work for us 🤷‍♂️... rather than obsessing over wording or arbitrary metrics."

And elsewhere, the mechanism they fear: "Engineers focused on small quick wins to move those metrics, rather than building what our users actually wanted." — https://posthog.com/newsletter/product-management-is-broken

**2. The career-progression page has a "Ways we do not help you progress" section I missed** (my earlier read of that file was truncated). Verified live:
> "**A checklist of things / a formal career progression framework.** This is self-interested by its nature, so creates the wrong incentives. The benefits of frameworks only start to outweigh their drawbacks when you need to start coordinating 100s of people."
> "**Fancy titles.** We don't have a wide range of titles."
> "**Getting a manager to progress you.** This gives too much power to managers... your motivation to progress has to be intrinsic to be sustainable."

At ~120 engineers, PostHog is explicitly below the scale at which they think a framework pays for itself. A dashboard that functions as a de facto levelling rubric is arguing against this page.

**3. No PIPs.** — https://posthog.com/newsletter/this-is-why-youre-not-shipping
> "We avoid performance improvement plans because it's demeaning for those affected, and excessively time-consuming for managers."

**Bonus dimension worth adding to the ranking** — Lior Neu-ner on what a successful engineering lead looks like: "You'll know you're successful if: **You can disappear for two weeks without affecting the quality and frequency of releases.**" — https://posthog.com/newsletter/tech-lead-failure-modes. That is a bus-factor/enablement metric, and it is the inverse of a hero-contributor metric.

---

## Corrections to §7 (structure and scale)

- **Headcount is 229, not 187.** The 187/47 figure I quoted from `product-engineer/culture` is stale. Current count from the site's own build data (`page-data/sq/d/2290419275.json`, built 2026-09-02) is **229 team members**, **54 live small teams**. Don't use the wider `staffProfiles` query (317) — it includes alumni.
- **~120 core software/product engineers** (137 have "engineer" in title; subtract Technical Support Engineer ×10, Developer Advocate, Developer Marketer). **The single largest job title in the company is "Product Engineer" — 67 people.** Also notable: **Context Engineer ×3**, a title that did not exist a year ago.
- Sanity check: ~120 engineers × ~200–310 merged PRs/weekday ≈ **2 merged PRs per engineer per weekday.** Any dashboard whose baseline expectation differs wildly from that is mis-calibrated.
- **`owners.yaml` is the real ownership system, not CODEOWNERS.** 28 `owners.yaml` files across the repo, 30 distinct `team-*` slugs; `.github/CODEOWNERS` is sparse (~100 lines, mostly security paths). There is a documented skill for it: `.agents/skills/establishing-code-ownership/SKILL.md`. Most-referenced owners: `team-analytics-platform` (20), `team-product-analytics` (19), `team-devex` (17).
- `products/engineering_analytics` is owned by **team-devex** (3 people).
- **Agent tooling scale:** `CLAUDE.md` is a 9-byte symlink to `AGENTS.md` (45 pairs repo-wide, CI-enforced). **257 `SKILL.md` files** — 88 in `.agents/skills/`, 164 under `products/*/skills/`.

---

## PostHog has already named your problem in a marketing doc

From their PostHog Desktop positioning (https://posthog.com/handbook/marketing/positioning/desktop.md):

> "**Problem:** Agents are shipping far more changes than your team used to. **Code review can tell you the diff looks right, but not whether the change did something meaningful** (and no one has time to set that up for every agent PR)."

That is the gap your dashboard should claim. Not "who is productive" — PostHog has written that question off — but "**of the ~5,000 PRs we merged this month, which ones did something**". Framed that way, the dashboard is on-strategy rather than in conflict with the locked decisions.

---

## How this changes the ranked dimensions

Two promotions, one demotion, one addition:

- **Promote "shipped-thing adoption" to #1**, above ownership blast radius. The desktop positioning quote plus the hidden-danger-of-shipping-fast essay mean PostHog's live concern is that throughput has outrun verified impact. This is the dimension they are actively short of.
- **Promote provenance/skills telemetry into Tier 1.** 93% of merged PRs declare which institutional skills shaped them. No commit-stats tool captures this, and it directly answers "how did agent leverage change what this team can do" without surveilling individuals. Aggregate it per team and per product area.
- **Demote raw PR throughput to a context strip, not a scored dimension.** PostHog has now said "more PRs isn't a good thing in and of itself" in a published post, abandoned OKRs over gaming, and locked "no per-developer cycle-time scores" into their own product. Three independent refusals.
- **Add revert rate and PR-size percentiles as counter-metrics**, exactly as PostHog computes them. These are the two quality proxies they chose themselves, so they need no justification to that audience — and their goal-setting handbook explicitly asks for counter-metrics ("X happens, but Y shouldn't happen").
